utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: First of all, since we both used the same language, if I could please ask you to pause after each of my questions to give the interpreters sufficient time to interpret our words and for everybody in the courtroom to understand what's going on. First of all, I would like to go through a sequence of technical questions in relation to your statements. You have given several statements and I hope we can go through this quickly. First of all, can you confirm that on the 28th of February of the year 2000 you testified before the investigative court of the military court, investigative magistrate?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I testified before Colonel Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to answer yes or no wherever possible. Please provide comprehensive answers only where absolutely necessary so that we may have a chance to go through this as quickly as possible. The interview was long; it went on from 9.00 in the morning until 2.00 in the afternoon, and you signed the minutes of that interview, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After this, between the 15th and the 25th of November, with certain interruptions, that was in 2002, you gave a statement to one of the OTP's investigators. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were interviewed and then a statement was drafted in Serbian; it consists of 22 pages and in English it consists of 28 pages. Would that seem to be right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the English version, but I believe you're right about the Serbian, 22 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that imply that you only read and signed the Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to the OTP investigators you were shown the statement you had previously given to the investigative magistrate of the military court. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While being interviewed by the OTP, at the end of your interview the investigator gave you a chance to make any amendments that you saw fit or perhaps to complement your statement. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would have had a chance to do that, but in a way I had no chance to do that whatsoever because all my words were recorded already and I just signed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you read the statement before you signed it, the one you gave the OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did read that one. As for the interview with Colonel Trifunovic, the magistrate of the military court, I did not read that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of November, 2003, you were interviewed -- or rather, were heard as a witness before the investigating magistrate of the district court in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was held in Belgrade. There was a request and I was heard before that magistrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You provided a brief statement or affidavit which is no more than a clarification of the statement you gave on the 28th of February to the investigating magistrate of the military court?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did not read that statement. I said that I did have certain observations to make about that one and the investigating magistrate did not give me an opportunity to go through that statement. I confirmed the authenticity of that statement in front of at least 10 attorneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if in that statement you gave to the investigating magistrate of the district court in Novi Sad, the one that you gave in Belgrade pursuant to a request that had been made, did you in fact correct only one detail in that statement which concerned your thoughts upon returning from Negoslavci to Sid?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I made certain observations about the time-line and events in that statement which seem to have been reversed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were these observations of yours recorded in that statement to the investigating magistrate in Belgrade or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be certain if they were or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you read that statement? Was it read back to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I orally presented some of my impressions about the previous statement, the one I'd given before Colonel Trifunovic, the investigating magistrate of the military court. I stated clearly that some of the facts were recorded wrong. I also said that certain questions were obviously trick questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will ask you some questions about the statement you made to the investigating magistrate from the district court in Novi Sad; it has to do with what we're talking about. If you can remember these things, please say so; if not, I can provide a copy of the statement for you to look at. You said this: "I fully abide by the previous statement that I gave before the investigating magistrate of the military court on the 28th of February, 2000. After I was presented with the substance of the statement that I made, I would merely like to express a number of reservations that I have relating to a particular sentence on page 12. The last sentence in paragraph 2, which states that: 'More or less all of us who were there knew about the fact that acts of vengeance were taking place against prisoners of war. I must say that, all things considered, this was my personal view and does not reflect the belief of all of those who were there.'" Did you state that to the investigating magistrate of the district court in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's part of the answer to the question that he posed. What was recorded here was recorded by the investigating magistrate. He had read the statement I had given before the acting magistrate of the military court. I said there and in my previous statement to the president of the chamber of the special court that this was my opinion and my opinion alone. I had no right to speak on behalf of anybody else or that group as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, sir, the statement we're talking about, did you sign it eventually? And what about the last passage before your signature, does it not state that this is all you have to say, you do not wish to read the transcript because it has been read back to you and it accurately reflects the oral statement that you made?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I said so while facing ten lawyers. And there was another question that I answered, and if you could please hear me out on this. I answered another question by the investigating magistrate of the special court -- no, the prosecutor of the special court who was in attendance. He asked me whether at the government session in Velepromet the agenda also included item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You were asked something by my learned friend from the OTP about this, and we are likely to go back to this at some point later on. Can we just please stick to the chronology of your statement. You were heard as a witness during the trial at the district court in Belgrade at the special war crimes court in Belgrade on the 20 -- on the 17th of December, 2004, and there's a transcript where your testimony was recorded. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've never had a chance to look at it, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You're an experienced security officer, and you're familiar with the provisions of the law on criminal procedure, particularly those governing the involvement -- the involvement of witnesses, the rights and duties of witnesses when testifying and so on and so forth. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As someone dealing with investigations as part of the security organisation and as someone who helped uncover certain war crimes and crimes in general, you are familiar with the role of witness in a criminal proceedings, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When giving statements you paid a lot of attention to every single word you uttered or every comment you made. You must have been aware of the potential consequences of any statements that you made or implications and ramifications for criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ask away, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you were extra careful about every single word you said, every single comment you uttered?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that. I would say that I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about you talking with my learned friend from the OTP from preparation of your testimony, did you go through all the statements and transcripts that we've just described?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can I take that to mean that together with my learned friends you've gone through all these statements prior to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I went through the statements, you mean? My statement before the war crimes chamber -- I did point out clearly in no uncertain terms that this was the most authentic statement that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm done with this set of questions and I'd like to move on to something else now. You were asked by my learned friend and you told him about your career as an officer, that you served with the armoured units and then you switched to security bodies. What I want to know about in particular is your involvement in the anti-terrorist struggle as -- during your time with the security organ. When exactly did you start fighting terrorism and what did your work really comprise?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, sir, my work with the security bodies of over 30 years was to protect the units, institutions, and command of the JNA from any threats. But roughly speaking, one-third of my entire career was spent fighting terrorism and the great results I achieved were in that area as a professional officer. I did not deal with political crimes. I helped uncover and prevent any acts of terrorism, acts of terror against the JNA and the armed forces. Following the death of the supreme commander, Josip Broz Tito, when this form of terrorism came to the fore, especially with ethnic Albanians setting up their own armed units, my task on behalf of the supreme leadership of the security administration was to tackle those issues. If I may just add one or two things, please. I achieved certain results, and I was particularly pleased personally when back in 1984 I tracked down Ernest Muriqi, a Turkish national, member of the JNA serving in the Ilirska Bistrica and Rijeka garrison who fired a hand-held rocket at the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the Turkish staff of the army. He fled back to Europe. He took refuge in Yugoslavia. He applied for Yugoslav citizenship. He got it, and he reported for military service. I uncovered his presence as a member of an illegal armed unit which as part of its platform as terrorist strikes. I asked him what weapons he had signed for, and he said the hand-held rocket launcher. I brought him in to the relevant investigating magistrate and then took him back to the court in Zagreb for -- in order for him to be investigating, questioned, and prosecuted. He said he was a member of the Red Front and Grey Wolves organisations back in Turkey. I recently read that Ali Agca, a member of this same organisation, was the man who attempted to assassinate Karol Wojtyla, the former pope. I can also give you some other facts if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We have to move forward in time to events more relevant for these proceedings. This is more to do with your career in the JNA, and I would like to ask you something about your particular powers and authorities. I would like to ask you something now. We're talking about terrorism and fighting the internal enemy. Can you please tell me the following: What about the security administration? When did fighting the internal enemy, as you put it, become a priority? Was it not in the years preceding the armed clashes in Slovenia, Croatia, and the break-up of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those tasks were always there for me; I was always aware of them. It was within this framework that I, for the most part, dealt with anti-terrorist activities which meant uncovering groups that were planning terrorist strikes. It's not my fault that the crime at the barracks in Paracin was committed, but I will give you one example of my involvement in uncovering that particular crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Which year was that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was back in 1987, the 3rd of September, 1987. I'm talking about the Paracin barracks. A crime occurred there and the public was informed about this crime by the -- by a representative of the army command in Nis. Aziz Kellmendi, a mad soldier had had a bad nightmare. Following that he picked up an automatic rifle and it was loaded. He went through three different rooms and killed a number of his fellow soldiers from the JNA. The highest security body of the JNA, the Koledjian [phoen], sent me, Colonel Vujic, to look into the matter. You saw the results. There was a terrorist group that was found out comprising a number of different people, and they were sentenced eventually. They were tried and sentenced. I won't say more about that now. Mr. Vasic, this sounds like a good thing, like a positive thing, but sometimes it's not. Sometimes the leadership doesn't really like these crimes being uncovered or criminals being tracked down. It all depends on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you suffer any consequences after you found out about the existence of this considerable terror group within the army?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was reprimanded by my secretary and my direct superior, the general at the time, said: You don't really like your supreme commander, do you? And I replied: And you are lying to your supreme commander. You are deceiving your supreme commander. This federal secretary soon retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While performing these tasks, fighting the irredentists and their troika, did you cooperate with General Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You must have enjoyed a relationship of professional trust because for a while you worked together closely, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that that was true. At the time I was in the centre for graduate military schools. I retired on the 1st of -- the 1st of -- or rather, in 1991 I received my first retirement benefit. I can tell you something else about my contribution in protecting the armed forces and trying terrorists. The last trial in Belgrade was a trial against terrorists involving a crime that I uncovered together with my subordinates. I submitted evidence and prosecution was instituted before the military court in Belgrade. Among the accused, there were soldiers of Albanian ethnicity, Slovenes, Croats, and there was supposed to be one Serb as well, however, he withdrew. They stood trial, and Nikola Barovic, an attorney well known to you, Tanja Petovar, Aleksander Lojpur, the late Branko Stanic are all attorneys-at-law who can testify about my involvement and my professional contribution in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that these soldiers were prosecuted. Were they taken into custody and put in detention prior to that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were first put in detention by the organs of the security and they were put in three-day detention and then that was extended.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that in late 1980s there was active struggle against terrorism and irredentism. In late 1980s as someone who was a specialist in fighting terrorism and irredentism, did you travel throughout Yugoslavia, did you take part in all activities of the security organs, of the army, and later on military districts?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call myself a specialist. I certainly had a lot of experience in this field, and this is where I achieved my greatest professional success. Yes, I was sent out on various missions to assist the security organs. I took part in investigations and proceedings before military courts in the territory of Croatia, Macedonia, Serbia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. As for my work, presidents of various military courts, such as Ivan Fumic, colonel and president of the court in Zagreb, who later became a Croatian justice minister, he can testify about my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. What would you say if I told you that one of your former colleagues from the security organs, General Imra Agotic, when testifying here in the Milosevic case said the following. Transcript page 23332, line 20 to 23. I will read it out in English and it will be translated to you. [In English] "I'm not talking about Kosovo. I am talking about the army. This was 1986, 1987, 1988 when people would come from the security administration, especially Colonel Bogdan Vujic, as a specialist under question mark" -- [Interpretation] I mean quotation marks. You heard Imra Agotic claim you were anti-terrorist specialist, in inverted cameras, under quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please put a question to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is this claim true, namely the claim that the job of uncovering terrorists was conducted by you in such a manner that you would take a list of soldiers containing names of Albanian soldiers, and then you would accuse them of being members of irredentist troika groups and file complaints against them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for General Agotic, he and I were colleagues, both of us, colonels born in the same republic, holders of the same citizenship, both Yugoslavia and Croatia. He was an ethnic Croat; I am a Serb. If this is what Imra Agotic stated indeed, I didn't hear about this, but I heard that Mr. Borovic asked Mr. Agotic here a number of times whether I was an honourable answer officer, and I will try to provide a an answer to this question whether I am an honourable officer or not. It is not my fault that Rahim Ademi, general, who was in the Detention Unit here in Scheveningen was a member of an illegal organisation which had terrorism as one of its aims. It is not my fault that I was involved on uncovering him. He was, in fact, given away by Albanians, his fellow compatriots, who said that he was involved in these activities. He was a security officer with a very high and responsible post in the Skeveni [phoen] garrison, and as such he inflicted great damage to the security organs. He posed a threat to the security organs as a member of an illegal organisation. I will show you a photograph. I personally was not involved in the prosecution of Ademi, Rahim. However, I gave a great contribution to his conviction, which is to say that I provided evidence, documentary evidence, about his illegal activity. As for conversations with him concerning various issues, I can show you that this was done by two Croatian officers who were designated for that duty precisely because they were Croats. I cannot assist Mr. Agotic in changing his opinion about me, but if necessary, I can give my position on Imra Agotic here before this Honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you had a code-name, which was Colonel Branko. Since all of your associates, your colleagues whom you mentioned here as persons who went to you -- who went with you to Sid and Negoslavci and so on, none of these had these code-names. Would you tell us why you alone were assigned one.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The witness unit here which takes care of witnesses, I asked two ladies who work there about their last names, and they told me that their last names were protected. Now, let me continue. In the law on the work of security organs it is set forth that in certain special cases, special instances and matters, certain actions are assigned a code-name and persons working in that operation can also be assigned a code-name. Why would I allow my person and my family to be at a risk just because I am involved in a certain operation? I do not want to allow this. Everybody was supposed to know who I was based on my involvement and my identity, and I had no way of protecting myself against them. In the statement that I took from Mrs. Vesna Bosanac, you can see clearly that my code-name is listed there as Colonel Branko. He insisted on me revealing my name, but I declined to do that. And there are several similar examples that I could give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is beyond dispute that you had a code-name. What I was interested in is this: You said that these code-names were generally assigned to people involved in a special mission or a task. What was your mission?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To investigate in the area of responsibility of Colonel Mrksic various crimes and criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was this name assigned to you specifically for this mission or did you have this name previously?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was assigned this name for this mission specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It's clear to me now. Thank you. You said that you retired from the post of chief of security within the graduate military schools. Tell me, please, is this the same level as the army general or, rather, the chief of security within the army?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not quite the same. I retired from the post of chief of security in the graduate military schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned names of some of your colleagues saying that they were chiefs of various departments and that you were given various missions to go to Begejci and so on. Would you please describe the organisational chart of the security organs at the time when you worked there.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I have already stated before this Trial Chamber, and I will repeat once again that I have a warning here before me issued by the military court which does not authorise me to reveal any state secrets. I know that General Aleksandar Vesiljevic perhaps spoke about this. He was here testifying, and he would be the best person to explain the organisational chart. He can also explain to you how groups came to be organised headed by Colonel Tomic Slavko, to which I belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is quite likely that the chief of security administration would be the best to explain this. However, we haven't had the honour of meeting him yet; this is why I put this question to you. The JNA doesn't exist any longer as an army. You were an officer of that army, so I don't see a conflict of interest here. I don't see why you are not authorised to reveal these things, and you are claiming that this is a state secret when this army does not exist anymore and this organisational chart is not current anymore.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it would be improper of me to do so, and I would like to ask you to spare me that question. Let me tell you this, though, I was engaged by Colonel Radovan Radivojevic, as I stated in my statement. He was the chief of one of organisational units in the security administration. He was subordinated to Vasiljevic, and he was also a member of the collegium of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Would you please tell us what was the chain of information from the military districts at the time towards the security administration.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, this chain of submitting information was uniform within the army. One chain of reporting or of submitting information existed within the state and a very similar one existed within the army. Everybody was supposed to report to their superiors, and then orders were going in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you retired in late December 1990, that your first retirement benefit came on the 1st of January, 1991. Was this the first mission you were assigned after you retired or you had some previous tasks?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any other tasks except for my civic duty. In my building, Colonel Kovacevic resided, commander of the armoured brigade in the Bjelovar garrison who was killed when the barracks was attacked. We waited for quite a long time for his corpse to be transported for the funeral. Since he and I lived in the same building, I was asked to assist with the preparations for his funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to this information that you learned through private sources, do you also have any official information about the attack of the ZNG against the Bjelovar barracks?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any official information. I only know what I learned through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that in October 1991 when you were assigned this mission to go to Begejci, Aleksandar Vasiljevic was chief of security administration. His deputy was?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simeon Tumanovic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you went to Begejci with a team established by the security administration with the task to investigate the commission of war crimes and other violations of the international law also on the part of members of Croatian army as well as members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Members of Croatian paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you performed these tasks in Begejci, how did you send your reports concerning the information you obtained by interviewing individuals there. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The results of my work in Begejci consisted of the statements provided by persons I interviewed. This was my method of work. I believe it to be the most transparent way to proceed and to show that the person drafting up the statement is fully transparent. This is why I always asked the persons I interviewed to write down their statements as their own statements and then we would write supplements and so on to the statements. These statements were included in a file. We had an officer there in charge of analytical work, and this officer later on processed these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that. But you and your colleagues, did you exchange information you acquired by interviewing these persons? Did you try to ascertain what other colleagues of yours knew?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not follow the standard procedure because the investigation itself and the results of the investigation need to be verified. In my opinion, the data can be verified only if there is coordination. If there are several members of the team, then the team leader should be the one to coordinate them, whereas some other people who are not directly involved need not be privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The tasks that you carried out at Begejci in addition to the duties from the security administration, there were also some representatives from the -- from the military district itself. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did they work independently from your group or were they, in fact, part of our [as interpreted] group?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They acted independently and were subordinated to General Milan Babic, although in some instances they probably overlapped. For instance, one person that was a suspect of a crime may have been, in fact, approached and interviewed by both organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that the chief of the 1st Military District was General Babic. What was Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic's role at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a specific answer to that question. However, evidently there were commands and headquarters at different levels. There were strategic units, and there were commands of strategic units as well as operational units, and these commands had senior officers running them as well as security organs. Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic must have belonged to one of these commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your statements you stated that he coordinated the work of security organs in the war-affected areas. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that was my impression and that's what I stated. My team leader, Colonel Slavko Tomic, was given his assignment at the headquarters where there was Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic. However, I cannot tell you who else was there at the time and I do not wish to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you say in your statements that Ljubisa Petkovic was in charge of receiving and putting up prisoners of war on behalf of the district -- of the military district?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic did distribute these POWs, and that was my impression. I also learned that one could not enter the war-affected areas or the combat areas without Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic's approval or permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me who set up the centre at Begejci and what the structure of the centre was, what its organisational structure was?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regulations governing the work of the JNA security bodies clearly indicate that the regulations applying international laws of war provide that the treatment of POWs is something that is regulated by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, and it was on this basis that I could conclude that there was an order on the setting up of POW camps and that pursuant to the order the duties of different participants in the process are provided in detail. I, myself, however, never saw any such order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether Begejci, just as Vukovar, falls within the area of responsibility of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Begejci was in the area of responsibility of the 1st Military District, and -- and it was some 100 kilometres away from the combat area, and that was in accordance with the regulations. However, the -- what the division of these different areas of responsibility were -- was is something that only the commander in charge of an area could know. Unofficially I learnt that the -- that Colonel Mrksic's unit was resubordinated to the commander of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That was not my question. My question was quite simple. Was Begejci, just as Vukovar, within the area of responsibility of the 1st Military District? Did they both fall under the same district?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I took this to be a trick question, and that's why I gave you an answer that I deemed could protect me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me phrase it this way: Shortly before the breaking out of the war operations, was Begejci, just as Vukovar, within the area of responsibility of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the guards brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, my question had to do with the 1st Military District, not the guards brigade.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Military District had a peace -- was a peacetime command. Your question had to do with the strategic command, whether it was the -- you had to distinguish in your question between the strategic and the operations commands. There were several units there which were operations unit and command -- combined units, and as -- since there were several corps and since there was the operations group under the command of Colonel Mrksic --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether all the units you mentioned now were subordinated to Commander Zivota Panic in the 1st Military District? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that. I cannot really tell you anything about the organisational matters as specific as I would like to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And how come you have knowledge of the corps and the existence of the corps?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- for instance, I heard about the existence of the corps from Arkan himself. I heard Arkan say -- I was with this commander and I -- do you know this general, Mr. So-and-so, and I would say: Yes. And he told me: Well, he's the commander of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So this was the source of your information. Thank you. Can you tell me in what way were the persons who were then questioned by security organs received at the Begejci centre?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I cast my mind back to those events and the time I worked there, I feel quite bad. Those were very hard times. I even have some regrets about being there, but at least I have the satisfaction of having given a contribution in terms of uncovering war crimes and perpetrators thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you try to do something to improve the conditions in the centre at Begejci?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to the commander of the camp who was a logistics officer. He told me that the farm was designated as the venue for a camp because it had been a camp during with World War II when German POWs were held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you submit your request to that effect in writing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to make sure that the electricity be introduced there. Later on representatives of different political organisations and TOs came over there, and I drew their attention to the low-living conditions and standards over there. And I indicated the possible consequences of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever observe violence being employed against the POWs there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would never have allowed that. I'm speaking frankly. I was always very strict when it comes to the application of the laws and regulations. I informed, for instance, Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic to take care that the law is applied or else consequences would ensue. That was something I told my superior, Colonel Tomic, as well. In the course of our work, we would board a mini-bus and start heading from the Zrenjanin barracks and then from the municipal building in Zitiste, and we had a lot of stops on our way and that's how we would come to Zitiste quite late. And we were able to deal with any tasks we had only as long as we had -- it was daylight and that was until 4.00 at the time. In the evening, we would go back to the barracks and that's why I, having been away most of the day, was not really informed about what was going on over there at the barracks -- at the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were there any visible traces of violence on the faces of the persons you interviewed? Was anyone beaten up or intimidated?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I stated in my statement, Franjo Kracak was the person I took a statement from. And after a while my impression was that members of groups actually agreed on the versions, colluded in giving their statements. I realised that they were indeed well organised, despite the conditions there, and that this was the way they tried to protect themselves, which goes to show that the conditions were not that bad after all because they were able to choose which room -- which bed to go back to once they are questioned, depending on who they wanted to talk to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ask them whether they were indeed abused?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I always ask them about that, and I was known to ask such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who was taken to the collection centre at Begejci, to your knowledge? Which people, from which territories?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood these people to be the ones who care -- who had carried arms. There was civilians there. There were family members as well. There would be a man with his wife and, in some cases, daughters. I understood them to come from the area of Pretpolje, that was the Vukovar defence area, from the villages situated between Ilok and Vukovar. They had all been armed. If, at a later point, you have any questions to put to me about Franjo Kracak specifically, I will answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My next question has to do with the following: What sort of information did you come by as far as the organisation of HDZ members is concerned into different staffs and the level of their organisation in the area of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through these interviews I learned that in all the different villages there was HDZ Crisis Staffs in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told me that Crisis Staffs of the HDZ were organised everywhere. What was the task of these staffs and how did they go about arming themselves in these villages and which time of year was this specifically in?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the process of arming started in the spring of 1991 and lasted until the start of combat operations or the outbreak of the armed conflict. As far as I was able to understand, members of the HDZ and of the HDZ Crisis Staffs first went out to sell automatic rifles that they had been given by Tomislav Mercep and his Territorial Defence staff of Vukovar, as it was initially called. They had to buy the weapons with monies, and weapons originally arrived from Hungary, Romania, and possibly from other countries as well. Some of them bore the insignia pointing to their countries of origin; others didn't. In the second phase with the start of the armed conflict and clashes against JNA units, they were given weapons. These staffs went about establishing units in charge of defending villages, making fortifications, trenches, and so on and so forth. Some of those were called up, were drafted into the units, and others were volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to a point in time prior to the period you spoke about. Before the HDZ started the arming process, did it set up units that were not armed in the local communes and villages and when was that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may have been so, but I wasn't interested in that aspect, which is a political one. I was more interested in the arming process, the crimes, and terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What role did Tomislav Mercep have to play in this process? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my conversations and my interview with Franjo Kracak, I obtained information on his role. He said he was a member of Tomislav Mercep's Crisis Staff, and he said that he had a number of assignments, firstly, to arm the Crisis Staffs in villages such as Sotin, Tompojevci, Cakovci, Mihalj. There is another village but I would have to use a map to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Which period of time are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was until the summer or until August 1991. And afterwards he was given a variety of assignments when the order came to fortify the defence lines, to fortify Vukovar's defence lines, he had a special permit allowing him to pass through minefields. He would bring with him a mine technician or an obstacle expert from Vukovar. He would bring this expert to the area in order to lay the mines and set up minefields in order to create zones through which the JNA tanks would not be able to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the mine technician? Did Franjo Kracak use groups of these even before the outbreak of clashes in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the close circle surrounding the leader of the Crisis Staff, Tomislav Mercep, and in this capacity was given special assignments, such as the setting up of the sabotage and terror groups whose tasks were to kidnap certain Serbs, bring them to the Crisis Staff headquarters where there was a prison, and some of them were even taken to the district prison in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, sir, all this happened before the outbreak of armed clashes in the summer of 1991, August 1991, to be more specific?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Franjo Kracak said that he used the secret route through the cornfield and across Bogdanovci twice in order to reach the village of Nijemci. He would then cross the JNA lines, the JNA combat lines in order to reach Ilok and the broader Ilok area where a number of special forces brought from Zagreb were stationed. Likewise, he was involved in organising groups that would stay in the area even after the arrival of the JNA. Eventually Franjo Kracak crossed the Danube and fled to Serbia and Vojvodina where he was carrying out certain assignments. That was where he was eventually caught along with the remaining members of his group, the group that he led. In addition to this, I can tell you that Tomislav Mercep had already established a personal group unit, a personal guards unit by this time which was stationed outside the town of Vukovar in Opatovac. They were stationed in number of huts there. They called them the youth club huts. He set up a command there, the guards command at the Nikola Subic Zrinski barracks which was bombed by the JNA air force planes. However, the guards unit had found out by this time that they would be attacked so they fled. The JNA units came into the area and sustained a great deal of casualties and losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Where did the guards unit flee to, do you know that, Mercep's guards unit, I mean?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took shelter at the Eltz palace, the Count Eltz palace in Vukovar. There was some special forces officers there, too, who had arrived from Zagreb. These were, for the most part, instructors training the guards units. There was the famous general, Ante Roso, still a major at the time, who was also there. And that's what I know about what was going on there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would just like to go back to one thing. During your conversations and interviews with Franjo Kracak, did you perhaps learn that houses belonging to Serbs had been blown up in Vukovar, Sotin, Ilok, between -- in the course of June and July 1991? Were there any such occurrences?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I learned something about that. This was described in Franjo Kracak's statement. I explained a number of names to him and a number of specific houses. I can't be very specific about this now unless you allow me to go back to my statement, then I can be more accurate about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If it's not too difficult, sir, please, would you care to just go through it. I suppose you only need to remind yourself about the names. Right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's all I'm looking for. I'm just looking for the right page. Zvonko Horvatic, Leko Gojani, Radocaj Josip were all members of his group at the time. As for Serbs whose houses were burned at the time, Torbica, Ilija; Kovacevic, Mirko; Draca, Dusko; Trkulja, Nikica. Another man called Trkulja, his first name is Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will not be requiring this anymore. What about when you questioned Franjo Kracak, did you learn anything about how the arming process was organised for Ilok and Erdut? Was he involved in those areas, too, in the setting up of military units in those areas?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the way I understood it. He was the commander of Ilok and Vukovar until the JNA units cut across at Babska. They reached the banks of the Danube, and Ilok's defence surrendered. I think this was on the 17th of October, and after that it was gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said the defence surrendered. Did you know anything about Franjo Kracak taking any weapons collected in order to be surrendered to the JNA by Vukovar defenders and those in the surroundings and that he took these weapons and gave them to the paramilitary units at Ilok?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I learned about that, too. This is another thing that was recorded in the statements of persons that I spoke to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever come across a person known as Stjepan Radas in these interviews with Franjo Kracak?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stjepan Radas was a commander of Mercep's guards unit, prior to which he had served as a JNA officer. I think he was a major in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the summer of 1991, did Franjo Kracak launch any attacks against JNA units or barracks?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Franjo Kracak was a true specialist. He was a mortar gunman; that was his military specialty. So he admitted that he had targeted the JNA barracks. He described the whole thing for me. He did not know if he had hit anything or not, but over a long period of time he had a large amount of ammunition available to him which he used to target military facilities, especially JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know where this JNA barracks was located, the one that was targeted by Franjo Kracak?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about the barracks, which barracks could it be? It was the barracks in which I was on the 19th and 20th of November. It's on the road leading to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the Vukovar barracks. Right? Okay. So now I know. Can you tell me about the terror operations that Franjo Kracak was planning to carry out in Vojvodina where he was eventually arrested.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not willing to share his assignments with me, but each terrorist and sabotage unit has its objectives as well as places where it is based. I think once they manage to break out, their objective must have been to reach the state border and flee to Hungary. Some of the members of this unit were found. They were hiding with members of different church or organisations in Subotica and Sombor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While interviewing members of this group and Franjo Kracak, did you learn anything about any Serbs who were detained in Vukovar during combat operations, especially in the police building and the All People's Defence building?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned a thing or two about that through our interviews, but I did not speak to any of the Serbs who had been detained, although it was my desire to get to speak to some of those, too. I do remember being visited by one of the directors at the Borovo company. He wanted to know if there was such and such a person among the POWs. He gave me a name, alleging that this was a person who had in the past physically mistreated him until he fainted on one particular occasion in a bunker in the building holding the headquarters of Tomislav Mercep. He knew this person because this person was a well known boxer from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: During these interviews, did you at any time learn if active and reserve units of the MUP, the National Guards Corps, and the HOS were ever mobilised and used to attack JNA units and institutions in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I obtained quite some information while carrying out my second or third assignment which entailed an interview with Ivica Bicanic. He worked as an administrator in Vukovar with Stipe Pole at the MUP. His task was to see that all the check-points of Vukovar's defence had sufficient supplies in terms of food, and he was also in charge of supplying communications equipment such as Motorolas. He told me about how the whole thing was organised. At one check-point you had MUP forces, ZNG forces, as well as HOS. They were acting in concert and under a joint command. They had different commanders. Some of the commanders were from MUP and some of the commanders were from the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And what do you know about this, the HOS, the Croatian defence forces, who were these people?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Croatian armed forces, the HOS. These were units belonging to -- well, I can't remember his last name. At any rate, he was killed in Zagreb. They had special assignments. They were a little like special police forces and they had special rules in their own defence areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a man who was a professional boxer and a well known person around Vukovar a while ago. Do you know what this person's name was, the person that that Borovo director was after?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was dropped on that occasion, but that was a long time ago and I can no longer remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn that Franjo Kracak remained in touch with Vukovar's defence throughout the combat operations in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he remained in touch with Tomislav Mercep's Crisis Staff for a long time. As far as I remember, he indicated in his statement that he had been to Vukovar twice on a mission and that he would return through the minefields in the defence area in order to reach the area in which he was supposed to carry out his assignment. In early November, after the village defences had fallen and after the units had been deployed between Ilok and Vukovar, he fled across the Danube. First he went to the bases that were already prepared along the Danube, and then he went on to Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was he an expert who was in charge of destroying JNA tanks at Vucedol and at Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't give most of the credit to him personally, but he does deserve some credit because he brought that person named Vlado who was an explosive expert. He was from a village called Jabukovac or something like that, somewhere near Ovcara. And Vlado was in charge of laying the mines. I talked to some of the POWs, and they referred to this place as the tank cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe we have enough time for one last question before the break. Do you know that he set up groups that were tasked with silently executing the remaining Serbs in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The last group that he led had this assignment. They would storm Serb houses, houses belonging to Serbs who they claimed were members of the SDS, and they would execute these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Was Franjo Kracak a member of Vukovar's defence Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of Vukovar's defence Crisis Staff at the time, for as long as Tomislav Mercep was still around, Marin Pliso, and other members of the Crisis Staff that he was close to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about after that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that he lost touch with these people and he worked on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you file any criminal complaints against Franjo Kracak's group with the district prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job was to conduct an interview to ascertain the facts, to make sure that the facts were in his statement, and then to forward the case to the military bodies for further investigation and prosecution. I do believe that he was eventually prosecuted, but I'm not sure about what went on later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. You submitted this to the military investigator, but that was accompanied by the criminal complaint, as is typical pursuant to our law.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't write a criminal complaint nor was I authorised to write one. The criminal complaint was written by lawyers typically, and the security administration had a lawyer working for it who was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question from this group. Do you know whether the members of this group that we are now discussing were exchanged for JNA officers, soldiers, and their families who had been imprisoned in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, whether that group was exchanged or not. I know from the press that an exchange was organised. I remember that Colonel Starcevic at the time was a member or perhaps a chairman of the exchange commission. And I took to him once a telephone book of the husband of Dr. Vesna Bosanac, Mr. Lavoslav Bosanac. I believe that he would have a use of this telephone book and that I could be accused of keeping it for some obscure reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if this would be a good time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic. We will have the first break now and resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would like to go to some details that we touched upon during the first parts of the cross-examination. Something remains unclear to me. The post that you retired from, which was the post within the graduate military schools, did you have a superior there within the security organ?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a superior. Up until that time, my superior was chief of security unit within the General Staff of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you yourself were?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I retired from the post of the chief of security organ. At the time a re-organisation had been carried out within the JNA and that was the then-organisational structure. I was chief of the security organ within the graduate military school's centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. So we clarified that. Another matter that I wanted to clarify is this: You said that you never filed criminal complaints against people you interviewed, but that rather that was done by a lawyer within the security organ?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, or a lawyer within the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did they write criminal complaints based on reports committed by you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A criminal complaint for prosecuting the group that we discussed, the group that was tried for terrorism, was submitted as well as draft indictment by the prosecutor who worked for the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was pursuant to the then-laws.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this person worked closely with the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, we have to distinguish between a criminal complaint and a request to institute or initiate investigative proceedings. These are two different things. So we have now heard that was done based on the reports that you submitted. I have something else that I would like to clarify, and it has to do with Mr. Lavoslav Bosanac. You said that you took his telephone book in order for it to be given back to him before he was exchanged. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He might have been already exchanged at that point in time. I took this telephone book which was with Vesna Bosanac and then was handed over to me. I in turn took it to Colonel Starcevic who was the president of the military portion of the commission for exchange of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Starcevic was a colonel at the time, wasn't he, and who were the other members of this commission?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I think that people on the commission for exchange were officers of the legal department within the security administration or perhaps people from the moral guidance department, and a JNA prosecutor must have been involved in this, or the JNA prosecutor's office had to be involved. This commission was established pursuant to the order of Federal Secretary [as interpreted] for People's Defence. The exchanges were conducted pursuant to lists and in accordance with the position taken by the prime minister and defence minister at the time; Mr. Panic was the prime minister. And the principle applied was all for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that prior to the decision taken by the prime minister, Mr. Panic, an operation was conducted by the security administration in order to collect or gather persons who would be exchanged for the JNA officers, soldiers, and their soldiers who had been imprisoned in the territory of Croatia by Croatian forces and were unable to leave the territory of Croatia. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I'm aware of is that the first person who was exchanged and had to do with my line of work in the Sremska Mitrovica camp was Dr. Sadika Bilus. She was head of one of the wards in the Vukovar Hospital, and she was among the first to be exchanged for the JNA pilots imprisoned in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was any of the other persons that you interviewed exchanged later on? Do you know of any such cases?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't know for which persons the group headed by Dr. Bosanac was exchanged for. Later I heard that these were citizens of Croatia who were in prison and had been prosecuted for espionage, terrorist acts, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We're trying to say that they were members of a group known as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name of the group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to turn to another topic. Concerning the transcript, the group was known as the Labrador group.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard subsequently that these were members of the Labrador group, that they were prosecuted and convicted. At the time I didn't know whether a final judgement had been passed in relation to Dr. Bosanac as well. I also didn't know whether these persons received a judgement or were perhaps exchanged before the judgement was passed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know at the time what were the tasks and activities of the Labrador group?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to read some statements, some judgements. And based on that I realised that explosives were found on many of them, and that based on expert analysis it was established that these explosive -- that this explosive had belonged to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back to the 19th of November, 1991. You told us that the security administration sent you to your new mission in Sremska Mitrovica where a new centre for reception of prisoners of war --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A camp for prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: A camp for prisoners of war from the territory of Vukovar. What was the goal in establishing this camp?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. The goal and the task must be written down in the order for establishing this camp. I didn't see this order. I received my orders from my immediate superior. My personal task was to interview prisoners of war in order to uncover crimes and those who committed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So the same task that you carried out in the camp in Begejci?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you told that persons who are not prosecuted because it is not established that they committed crimes would be exchanged for the JNA members?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the exchange lists were drafted up immediately. I remember that it was first the medical personnel who was exchanged; later on it was some civilians. There was no reason to prosecute them. They were exchanged for some Serbs from the territory of Croatia, or perhaps for some soldiers who were in prisons or in camps in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Sremska Mitrovica you were told that your team would receive some additional personnel from the security administration. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that the tasks associated with interviewing these persons were conducted by the officers of the security administration and officers of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to put that question to General Aleksandar Vasiljevic and to put questions to me which pertain solely to my tasks within my scope of authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. When carrying out your tasks interviewing these persons, did you see any members or representatives of civilian authorities of Baranja, Slavonia, and Srem taking part in this kind of work?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them. And I also had occasion to meet again the minister of justice in the government of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem, Mr. Vojin Susa. He brought a group of lawyers with him. I believe that there were four or five, maybe even six of them. They audited -- or rather, supervised our work, as far as I'm concerned at least. I don't know who else's work they supervised, but definitely mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that when you were given this task you were told that a new POW camp was being established, that a large number of POWs was expected. Did they, when telling you this, use the term a large number of Ustashas? Was this the term used by the Supreme Command and the officers of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. The first time I heard this term used was in the area of responsibility -- or rather, at the command headquarters of Colonel Mrksic and also in the meetings with Major Sljivancanin. I also heard this when Colonel Tomic asked Major Sljivancanin how many captured Ustashas there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see any order from this period of time or any report of the command of the 1st Military District which dealt with the captured persons?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have occasion to see or hear of any such order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can add that the head of the Sremska Mitrovica camp was appointed by the head of the security administration. I stated so in my statement. This was Colonel Jugoslav Maksimovic. He also signed his name and his title as camp commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And he was subordinated to the head of the security administration?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you described to us how you arrived in Sid. What would you say if I told you that Colonel Kijanovic, whom you mentioned yesterday as a member of your group, claims that back in Sid you were declared to be the head of this group?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to face him here before this Trial Chamber and before you, face Colonel Kijanovic so that we can harmonise our statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that Colonel Tomic, whom you described as the head of the group, was at that time a man of advanced age, unlike you, and that he came to your group as a volunteer and not at the request of the security administration as you, would you then accept my claim that it was you who headed this group and not Colonel Tomic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not accept that. And I can explain this and give you some facts, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you not the most experienced individual in that group invited by the security administration precisely because of your prior experience in fighting the internal enemy. Unlike you, Colonel Tomic was a participant of World War II.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not accept this position. Colonel Tomic had worked in the security organs for many years. He fought in the war, yes. Both of us were born in Western Slavonia. He was born a bit closer that Jasenovac than I was; however, both of us were from that general area. He has experience from World War II, perhaps greater than mine, when it comes to Jasenovac, Ustashas, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you are claiming that the security administration appointed a volunteer to head the group rather than an expert who was asked to come from retirement in order to take part in this?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the law on All People's Defence, if you research this in some detail you will find that the head of the security administration and the head of the security organ within an army and those at his level, such as chief of navy and chief of air force, are authorised to issue an order to establish operations groups with special tasks, that these groups can comprise volunteers and active-duty members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I just interrupt for one moment. With the utmost respect, my recollection is that the question was put that Colonel Tomic was a volunteer and whether this witness knew it. The reply was that he did not know basically one way or other that Tomic was the leader of the group. The situation is that my learned friend then says in the question at 40.13: "So you're claiming that the security administration appointed a volunteer to head the group rather than an expert?" He is not claiming that; he is saying simply that he does not know if Tomic is a volunteer or not. And it is a proposition that is being placed before the Court by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe the difficulty lies in the linguistic aspect, in the interpretation. I don't think the witness said that Mr. Tomic was a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Tomic was a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I may, Colonel Tomic was also summoned to the meeting, first at the security administration and that at Colonel Radojevic's because Colonel Tomic was also working in the security administration where Colonel Radojevic was serving, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you wish to claim that Colonel Tomic never stated that he had reported as a volunteer to the group?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was there on a voluntary basis as well because I was part of the reserve force and was asked to state whether I agreed to join the group. I was, therefore, asked to come of my own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The question put to you was: Did Colonel Tomic ever tell you that he was a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in those terms, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Very well. What would you say if I told you that Colonel Tomic, while he was alive, said that he received a phone call and that he was supposed to go to Sremska Mitrovica and that you were, in fact, the head of the group?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was his right to defend himself. If Colonel Tomic were here now today, of course we would look each other in the eyes and compare our statements. I can also tell you that prior to his death, which was I believe about one month before he died, Colonel Tomic invited me and another colleague of ours to visit him after surgery. He told me at the time: You have to apply to be a witness. And my reply to him was: Perhaps you will live to be a witness, too. In this conversation of ours, he told me -- or rather, he indirectly indicated that he wasn't telling the truth. And I'm sorry to have to tell you this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you set out from Sremska Mitrovica to Sid, you said that you were driven in a military vehicle that was signed for by Colonel Kijanovic. What sort of a vehicle was it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the vehicle of the Zastava make, and we popularly call it in Serbia Kec. I can tell you that Colonel Kijanovic signed up for the vehicle and that the vehicle belonged to Colonel Radojevic's unit, that he was the one who had to account for the fuel use, that he was the one who had the vehicle serviced. I can also tell you that Colonel Kijanovic was retired only from the Yugoslav army and not from the JNA, as I had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In response to the question put by my learned friend, you said that upon your arrive in Sid you pulled up the vehicle and that Colonel Tomic went over to Colonel Petkovic's and you stayed behind in the car. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was not the only one left in the vehicle. There were three other senior officers with me, and they will also have to state their opinion and the truth. And that would be my appeal, that they should be invited to state the truth here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the names of these -- could you tell the names of these officers?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Kijanovic, Colonel Kijanovic; Slobodan Stosic, captain first class; Stevan Mirkovic, warrant officer. When Colonel Tomic returned and told us that we would be given our assignment by Colonel Mrksic and that we were to go to the command post at Negoslavci next, he also told us that to that end we would be escorted by an armoured combat vehicle that would go ahead of us, as I stated in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I were to tell you that Colonel Kijanovic states that all -- together, all of you went to see -- with Colonel Kijanovic, you went to see Colonel Radojevic. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that General Babic's and Colonel Petkovic's command post was housed in the post office building?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said that the headquarters of Colonel Petkovic were in the post office building in Sid. That's probably his command post. We met with Colonel Babic during the night or in the early morning hours as we were coming back from Negoslavci. That was between the 20th and the 21st of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you come across him in the post office building?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the post office building on the floor where Colonel Petkovic had his office, although he was not there. Only Slavko -- only Colonel Slavko Tomic went into the office and stayed there for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did General Babic have his office in this post office building that you entered?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, although it may have been the case. I did not understand it to be his office, but rather as a room where General Babic would sometimes be present, where we had our coffee, and some cognac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was there a desk at which General Babic was seated?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was sitting on the desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us then where General Babic's headquarters was?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you expect to find General Babic there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. When we entered the building, Colonel Tomic greeted General Babic first. Shortly afterwards I went to Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic's office. He came out of the office to greet us, and I don't know who else was there in Colonel Petkovic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you have any professional dealings with General Babic?
