utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not General Babic's subordinate, except for the fact that I was duty-bound to consult him, as in fact I did, and to say hello to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My question was whether you had cooperated on some matters.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We may have cooperated at the time when we were officers holding the ranks of lieutenant-colonel and colonel. He used to work for the security administration once, just as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In late 1991, did you have any professional dealings with him at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that I was ever given any assignments from him, nor could he have given any to me without the knowledge of Aleksandar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether at the time in the post office building in Sid the elements of the counter-intelligence service of the air force were to be found there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I did not see any such members there, except for the fact that I had heard of a colonel, and I can't remember his name now. He must have been in that building as well, but he -- although he wore an air force uniform, he must have belonged or been a member of Colonel Petkovic's staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that after this brief stay in Sid you went over to Negoslavci. Did you find out what your task was going to be as -- already in Sid, or was it something that could be derived from the tasks that were given to you while you were leaving Begejci to go to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the statements I gave, including the one before this Tribunal, I stated that Colonel Tomic stated in Mitrovica that he had spoken to Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic, who told me that we were supposed to go over to Sid immediately to see him, that the fall of Vukovar was imminent, that there would be a large number of prisoners, and that we would be charged with organising -- with organising the taking in of prisoners and placing them in the camp. The only thing we were told by Colonel Tomic was: Lads, we're moving ahead. We're supposed to report to Colonel Mrksic in Negoslavci, where we would be given our mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While Colonel Petkovic was telling you what your assignment would be, as you put it just now, did you inform your superiors in the security administration of the task given to you by Colonel Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive my mission from Colonel Petkovic. I did not see him on this occasion except when I was on my way back. It was then that -- or rather, on this occasion, only Slavko Tomic went to see Colonel Petkovic, and I can vouch for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My question to you was whether your superiors in the security administration were aware of the fact that your group was given a mission from Colonel Petkovic and that you were relocated.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. Colonel Tomic and Colonel Petkovic may have been informed of that. Since both of them are dead, I stand by what I said before. However, there are other eye-witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as an officer of the security administration of many years and as part of a group that was sent by the security administration, could you have been given an assignment by someone else without letting the administration know?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody could give us any such assignment because our group was acting exclusively on the orders of the chief of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The assignment you referred to that you say was given by Colonel Petkovic through Colonel Tomic, which consisted of taking prisoners of war in when you were called from Sid?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to take part in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was this assignment identical to the assignment you were given in Negoslavci, the reception and evacuation of POWs?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you 100 per cent -- an answer with 100 per cent certainty. Under the rules of international laws of war, the task of the military police is set forth, but the task of the security bodies in relation to the POWs is not provided for. However, there is one item wherein it is stated that the setting up of the first camp and of a POW camp is something that is to be governed by the regulations issued by the federal secretary. Indirectly this means that there are such regulations, although we cannot see any here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My question had to do with one matter only. You told us that Colonel Tomic had relayed to you the task given by Colonel Petkovic to the effect that your group was to go to the Vukovar area to receive and evacuate POWs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To take part in receiving the POWs and to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In terms of the substance of the task, is it not identical to the task given to you in Negoslavci, to take the POWs in or to receive them and evacuate them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will refer you back to my statement in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will. You told us that you were given an assignment by Colonel Petkovic to go to the Vukovar area -- or rather, before that to go to Sremska Mitrovica and then to Vukovar with the task of participating in receiving and evacuating prisoners of war. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To assist in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you receive an identical task, essentially, to this one in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What sort of task were you given in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already stated before this Honourable Chamber and in my statement, Colonel Mrksic was given the assignment . That was my understanding. He relayed his task to Major Sljivancanin. Major Sljivancanin, in turn, informed us of this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you was whether, in essence, these were identical tasks, not -- I'm not asking you who or whether anybody relayed that task to you, but rather whether these were essentially the same tasks.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a specific answer because I did not receive the task from Colonel Petkovic. I had heard of the task from Colonel Tomic, who had relayed it to me, and it had to do with assisting in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in terms of its substance, the task given to you by Colonel Tomic, was it essentially the same to the task given by Colonel Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard of the task from Colonel Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, how is my learned friend [sic] to answer that question if in actual fact he wasn't privy to what Petkovic said to Tomic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a valid point, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've just asked the witness what Colonel Tomic had told him about what he had heard from Colonel Petkovic what their assignment was, and was this assignment essentially the same as the one they had received in Negoslavci. This is the fifth time I'm asking the question, and I can't seem to receive a proper answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I didn't receive the task myself, I've only heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour, thank you. But I'm asking the witness whether what he heard on the mission was the same as the assignment they had been given at Negoslavci. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He answered that fairly specifically a little earlier. The question was whether he was to assist or to do it or whether the group was to merely assist or to do it is the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't think the witness was sufficiently clear in answering my question, and that's why I'm trying this hard. I'll try it like this. Which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understood it clearly. I think the difference, in simple terms, is whether it was Colonel Mrksic's task or whether it was this group's task. Is that not the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not quite. Your Honour, I didn't get to whether this was Colonel Mrksic's task or not. And once we've done that, we can go back to this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that Colonel Mrksic got an assignment. Did you actually see him receive an assignment or an order? Did you hear about him receiving an assignment, or is that just an inference that you are making?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he had received an assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Heard from whom?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Major Sljivancanin. He said: There is a plan, which meant there are sufficient forces to carry out this mission. I took that to be a reference to us as well. I took that to include us, because we were also forces contributing to the completion of that task or assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you told whose plan this was, whose mission this was, and who ordered this plan to be designed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin didn't share that with me. I don't know if he knew or not, but obviously there was some sort of plan, because otherwise there would have been no plan to carry out, would there? It would have required an enormous amount of resources and forces to carry out a task like that. A camp needed to be organised at Sremska Mitrovica to receive these people. This required coordination between at least two different ministries: The justice ministry and the defence ministry. The task had to be carried out, physically carried out, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you see an order to that effect, or is that just an inference that you're drawing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see a physical order, but I saw the way things were organised and that had implications that I described, both in my statement and my testimony before this Trial Chamber. There must have been a plan; that much is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How then do you know that Colonel Mrksic was the one who received this assignment? You didn't see the order, you had no idea which particular body had issued this order.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The POWs were within Colonel Mrksic's area of responsibility. The building inside which the POWs were being kept was within Colonel Mrksic's area of responsibility. It was being guarded by Colonel Mrksic's military police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll come to that. But wasn't this also General Zivota Panic's area of responsibility? Wasn't this also Mile Babic's and Ljubisa Petkovic's area of responsibility? Wasn't this also Aleksandar Vasiljevic's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as a professional soldier I know what "area of responsibility" means. The whole of Yugoslavia was an area of responsibility protected by its constitution. Everybody was responsible for something, as you know. You have a brigade-level unit or an operations group, and each of these would have their own areas of responsibility. Colonel Mrksic I'm sure knows exactly what his own area of responsibility comprised and which specific units. I'd be hard put to specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, when you received your assignment from Colonel Petkovic, which was relayed to you by Colonel Tomic, what exactly did he do? What were you supposed to do now?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were supposed to assist. To assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What does that mean, "to assist"?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means to go on doing what we had been doing. I did tell you that some of the people worked in a way which was less than honourable. I did what I took to be my task. That was what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand you. What exactly was your job there? You didn't share that with us. What specific steps were you meant to take?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were meant to assist, to give them a hand. You realise what my task was about. Colonel Tomic spoke to everyone and transferred his responsibility to me, saying that I would be in charge of the boarding or separation of POWs at the Velepromet facility. I accepted that. I accepted that to be my assignment, and I made sure that my assignment was carried out in the way I have been described before this Trial Chamber, including the additional explanations that you have requested and that I have provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What you've just told us you did, would that fall under the definition of reception and evacuation of prisoners of war? Do you think this would be encompassed by that definition?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of the part that relates to me and no one else, when I said: I am taking over command, I personally am taking over command. Because that's what I told Mr. Sljivancanin's subordinate officer. If I may, I would also like to tell you how Major Sljivancanin relayed this assignment, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about the substance of your assignment. We'll get to all these other things. Thank you, sir. While you were at Sid, were you informed that members of the National Guards Corps and other paramilitary formations of Croatia were hiding in the hospital and elsewhere in Vukovar in a bid to avoid capture?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing at Sid, nothing at Mitrovica. We heard nothing about these things. I had no idea where Negoslavci was, to begin with, geographically speaking, until I got there. I had no idea about what our assignment would be after we had been told by Colonel Mrksic and after our assignment was relayed by Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Colonel Tomic went to see Colonel Petkovic and then he was back, at least that's what you claim. Upon his return, did Colonel Petkovic not assign to you a group of officers from the security administration, the 1st Military District, to go with you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear where.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he did not give us a group of officers. He gave us an armoured combat vehicle to drive us to Colonel Mrksic's command post. Excuse me, sir, if you could please try to pay attention, and then perhaps you may grasp my answer. We found Colonel Petkovic's operations group there once we arrived in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about when you gave a statement to the investigating magistrate of the military court on the 28th of February, 2000. You said something else, didn't you, that you left Sid in two vehicles, two cars, and in the other car there was a group of officers assigned to you by Colonel Petkovic. That was what you said at the time. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what was taken down in that particular statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought that we had established a practice that if in actual fact there is going to be a challenge about what has been said on a previous occasion that the document should be shown on each and every occasion and the reference be given so both sides know exactly to what we're referring. It's unfair on the witness if this is done in this way. I would merely ask that, as before, a document is produced and a reference given.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I can do that for my learned friend, no problem at all, but I just wanted to hurry things along, especially since the witness does not seem to be challenging the fact that he did say that. For my learned friend's reference, the page number is 3 of the B/C/S of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Mr. Vasic, I know that this was recorded, but that wasn't what I said at the time to the investigating magistrate. I said that an armoured combat vehicle was driving ahead of our vehicle. Please excuse me for what I'm about to say. Slavko Tomic was sort of joking and was saying things like: I said that we drove all the way to Negoslavci in an armoured combat vehicle. And what you should do now is check his statement, not mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I'm giving you as free a hand as possible in this cross-examination, but if you want the Chamber to take any accurate notice of any differences of account, you need to go through the procedure of having the witness look at what was said before, agree what is there, agree it's different, and then the witness add any explanation. Now, that hasn't been done. You know what the witness's present statement is about these events. Okay? So if you want us to notice a difference, do it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your guidance, Your Honour. That is precisely what I'm about to do. Can I have the usher's assistance, please, and I would like to show the witness a copy of his own statement to the military court, 28th of February, 2000, page 3. I've highlighted the relevant portion for you. For my learned friend's benefit, as well as that of the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have read --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my learned friend and the Chamber, this is page 3 also.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please slowly read out loud the passage that I have highlighted.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I've read the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, please, read it out loud so that we can have it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Once in Sid we reported to Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic, who was coordinating the work of the security body of the 1st Army. He was in charge of the reception, selection, and distribution of prisoners of war. The only person who talked to him was Slavko Tomic, while the rest of us waited in the car. He assigned to us his own operations group, and we drove off in two cars across Tovarnik to the village of Negoslavci. Once we reached the command post of Operations Group Jug, we reported to the commander, Colonel Mrksic."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That appears to be quite a clear statement. Did you, in fact, state this, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I will tell you exactly what the catch is about this whole thing. All of this is true, but the bit that says: "He assigned to us," "he assigned," Colonel Petkovic, to us an armoured vehicle which drove off ahead of us across Tovarnik all the way to Negoslavci, that's what it should say. Once there, we found Colonel Petkovic's operations group in the area; they joined us on this mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you're still claiming what you're saying now. You said the very same thing to the investigating magistrate, and the way he recorded these matters was fallacious or he simply got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I can tell you about this, too. When we spoke to Colonel Tomic he was sort of joking, and he said: I was the one who told them that we drove there in an armoured combat vehicle. Then I asked him: Why did you say that? And he said: Well, I just wanted to avoid having to mention Colonel Kijanovic driving one of those vehicles belonging to the security administration. I wanted to talk my way around the fact that he was the one driving us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And when you were interviewed by the investigating judge in Novi Sad and when you gave the corrections which we have mentioned here, you did not point this out, did you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this cannot be corrected, Mr. Vasic, and you know this fully well. What is once written down cannot be corrected. This can just be clarified later on. You will have occasion to see other witnesses here, and you will hear from them, and then you'll be able to make your conclusions as to whether I'm telling the truth or not. Mr. Vasic, I wasn't alone there. There were very many people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not be needing the statement any longer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that you arrived in Negoslavci and found there this group belonging to the security organ -- or rather, the security organ of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the commander of this group was Muncan, Dragan. He might have been a major already, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did this group become a part of your group or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were with our group, but they also carried out some assignments of their own, as they told us they had been there already for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that they had some assignments of their own. Does this mean that they also carried out some assignments which they received from your group?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They could not have received any assignments from our group because they did not belong to our group, and this would violate the subordination principle. I don't think that General Mile Babic would have consented to this. In addition to that, I also think that Aleksandar Vasiljevic would have objected to this, too. He was the most senior officer within the security administration, and he was certainly authorised to supervise and monitor the work of any of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And he could have ordered for this group to be joined to your group. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he could have, but only in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you came to the headquarters of the Operations Group South on the 19th of November at around 2000 hours. Can you describe to us where this command post of the operations group was in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the village of Negoslavci. The building, I would describe it as a villa, was on the left of the road leading to Vukovar. It had two storeys, if I remember correctly, and a well-built basement. I only stayed on the ground floor, which is where our operation -- or rather, which is where the operations room was. And this is where Colonel Mrksic met with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any other rooms there or did you see just this one room that you called operations room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another small room which was on that same level, perhaps a few steps above, but on that floor. I didn't go into any other rooms, nor do I know what the floor looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And what was there in that room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An operations map and a desk -- or rather, a table and some chairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Why did you go into that room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received a part of our briefing there, what Colonel Mrksic had to say to us about the tasks of the brigade, about the combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So he told you this in this small room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And when you were in the operations group, when was that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we greeted him and Colonel Pavkovic and Lieutenant-Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- who was the Chief of Staff of Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned Colonel Pavkovic, was he a representative of the Supreme Command there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. And this is the capacity of his that I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name. This had to do with Colonel Pavkovic -- or rather, he was a colonel at that time.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am only referring to the ranks as these persons held at the time, at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you were also given some assignments in the small room. And who was present there when this situation in Vukovar was described to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomic, Kijanovic, myself, Stosic, also security officers from the group of Major Muncan, or Captain First Class. Occasionally Major Sljivancanin would be present as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the name that wasn't picked up was the name of the Chief of Staff of Colonel Mrksic. I don't think that has been clarified in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. You are quite right. I did not register that. I believed that another name was a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat who was the Chief of Staff of Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Miodrag Panic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 19th you spent some time in Negoslavci and then set out to Vukovar later on. On the 19th of November, did you see anywhere in Negoslavci the chief of the security administration, Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him anywhere, even though I expected to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about his deputy, Mr. Tumanov?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him either. I didn't expect to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us then how come you expected to see Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed this task to be so highly responsible that it had to warrant the presence of the chief of security administration in terms of its operative value. When it comes to prisoners of war, this was a complex task, and the most senior officers, the most responsible officers had certain tasks in relation to this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that Mr. Vasiljevic was in Negoslavci that evening? Did you hear that he stated so himself when testifying in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that, and I would have liked to have seen him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When asked by my learned friend, I believe that you said that Colonel Mrksic, in describing the situation in Vukovar to you, also said that he had met with Marin Vidic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And that Marin Vidic signed a document on the surrender of Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that Mr. Mrksic said this to you? Because the position of my client is that he had never with Mr. Vidic in Vukovar, that Mr. Vidic never signed any document on general surrender of Croatian forces, but that the surrender, rather, unfolded in agreement with local commanders, such as the instance in Mitnica where Colonel Pavkovic negotiated with Croatian commanders.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe that I did not hear this there, at the command post. And I can further claim that I did hear this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who did you hear this from?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had heard this from Colonel Mrksic. If Marin Vidic, as a representative and as a plenipotentiary as an authorised person of the Croatian government and President Tudjman at the time signed a document on surrender, then he could have submitted it only to Colonel Mrksic, who was the most senior commander in that area of responsibility. This is how the international laws of war regulate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you have no information as to whether Marin Vidic signed a capitulation document -- or rather, a document on surrender of Croatian forces Do you know whether such a document was ever signed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never talked to Marin Vidic as a prisoner of war; this was done by Colonel Slavko Tomic. Had I interviewed them, I would be in the position to give you a very explicit answer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Certainly. But tell me, please, what did Mrs. Bosanac tell you about this? Was she aware of the activities of Marin Vidic in relation to the surrender of Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, she said that Marin Vidic was what he was, that he was a member of the main Crisis Staff, and that she didn't like it when Marin Vidic moved the Crisis Staff into the hospital. I would have to consult the statement written by Mrs. Bosanac. However, when they took this statement away from me, I never saw it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we will get to this statement later on and the interview held with Vesna Bosanac, but we're now dealing with the events in Negoslavci. When discussing the situation in Vukovar, was it ever mentioned that there was an order to collect the prisoners of war in order to carry out a triage and perhaps exchange them for the members of the JNA? Are you aware that such a request ever came in from the security administration?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Our first task was the evacuation from the combat area. This is what the rules envision and only after that can a selection process be conducted. If somebody said that a selection process was conducted right there on the spot, then that person made a mistake and -- and abused the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you find out there at the command post that the main tasks of the JNA were to lift the siege of the barracks and to establish law and order?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this from the media. I heard this from Colonel Mrksic when he told us what mission his brigade had. He told us that the brigade had established its mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When asked by my learned friend, you said that you had heard that 600 people had been put out of action. Is that the number of the members of the Operations Group South who were wounded and killed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I don't think that that's the right number. I never learned of the right number. I only know what Colonel Mrksic said. Now, whether he only referred to the brigade or to other units within his area of responsibility, I don't know. He said that about 600 people had been put out of action, that there were many persons who were killed, a lot of subordinate commanders had been killed. I said so in my statement, but another sentence of his is missing from the statement. It should not be taken literally. This was just a statistical fact, you know, when one is talking about the number of people put out of action, then what they have in mind is this general number of members and subordinate commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know if this would be a good time for our break. I can't see the clock from where I'm standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it's a convenient time, we can break now, Mr. Vasic, and we will resume at 10 to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I'm sorry for troubling Your Honour. Your Honour, there's just one matter; I'm sure it was unintentional. But one of the questions that was put by my learned friend was: "Did you ever hear that Mr. Vasiljevic was in Negoslavci that evening? Did you hear that he stated so himself when testifying in the Milosevic case?" The answer was: "No, I didn't hear that, and I would have liked to have seen him there." Well, we have searched the record of the Milosevic transcripts, obviously we've had to do it at speed, but there is nothing that we can find to suggest that that was ever said in the Milosevic trial. Could my learned friend refer me, please, to the transcript page where that is said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank my learned friend. That was my mistake. Witness Vasiljevic stated that in his evidence in -- before the war crimes chamber in Belgrade. At any rate, the witness did not hear of this, and it is not relevant for my further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that, Mr. Vasic. Well, if you would like to carry on now. We take it you'll be finishing today, will you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Your Honour, I will not be finishing today. Although the Defence teams did their best to divide different topics, we will not be able to finish today as much as we have tried. I believe that this witness covers a number -- a vast number of topics and we will need more time for our examination. The Defence will do its best --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, that is an issue as to the total time in respect of this witness. We certainly understand his importance, and we've given -- been giving you a free hand, but we're not going to be able to afford to allow you a day and a half or two days and then to find other counsel wanting time as well. What is the anticipated total time for yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe I should be able to finish my examination in one and a half sessions tomorrow. Perhaps I would require only the first session tomorrow depending on the witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will ask Mr. Borovic what is his anticipated time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, everything depends on the witness's answers that he will give today and tomorrow. It might even be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "very brief"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that if the answers will be adequate in terms of the questions put today by Mr. Vasic, then I will not be covering these questions myself, and I will be able to finish tomorrow. I suppose, at any rate, I would take an hour and a half, because we did our best to honour judicial economy. And as far as this Defence team is concerned, I don't think there will be any difficulty there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can tell you at this stage that I need two sessions of one and a half hours each. This witness has touched upon a number of interesting topics, and I cannot be -- give you a definite answer because this witness is a very important witness for us. But I believe that I would be able to finish in two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the view of the Chamber, cross-examination should finish at the end of the first session on Wednesday. That means that you will need, I think in fairness to your colleagues, to speed up a little, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Borovic, who seems to have very little interest in the evidence of this witness, if one thinks about it, I don't think your client's been mentioned, I think you could become quite brief. And Mr. Lukic will have whatever is left, so he will be looking over your shoulder, Mr. Borovic. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, we were discussing the assignments you were given in Sid and Negoslavci. If the task that Colonel Tomic received in Sid is, for the present purposes, designated as task A and the other one task B, can you tell me whether A equals B or, in fact, does not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I have repeatedly told you what my understanding of the assignment given in Sid was. In my statement and before this Chamber, I relayed the substance of the task received at Colonel Mrksic's command post in Negoslavci. I stand by what I stated earlier; that was that the task was given to Colonel Tomic. Now, whether he was given some other assignment in addition to this one, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My question was quite clear. If what was relayed to you by Colonel Tomic is designated, for the present purposes, as A and the other one in Negoslavci B, does A equal B or not? Because this is something you were supposed to inform your superior at the security administration of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the answer has been similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, Mr. Moore was on his feet. I was waiting for the translation to finish. We have had repeatedly the witness's precise description of the task given him. Really, that's it. I don't think you can just keep going at that. You have asked him about the other task; you got his answer on that. Now, later on we can work out what the difference is, if there is one. Okay? So if you would move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will move on and ask the witness whether he informed his superior at the security administration of the task of the assignment he was given at Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He's already answered that; he's told you "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is the witness aware of the obligation to -- in case he receives a different assignment from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... he's told you he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- from someone else that he has to inform his superior thereof.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received the assignment from Colonel Mrksic, and the assignment was relayed to me by Major Sljivancanin. That's as far as I'm concerned. Colonel Tomic relayed his assignment to me. Colonel Mrksic relayed his assignment to Colonel -- to Major Sljivancanin. I, myself, was informed of the assignment by Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, were you duty-bound to inform your superior at the security administration of the order relayed to you by Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My superior, Colonel Slavko Tomic, was present at all the meetings and was able to hear what our assignments were. Now, whether he knew something more about the evacuation plan for the POWs and about the actual operations situation in the area of responsibility of Colonel Mrksic, this was not something that he made me privy to. He only authorised me to implement the assignment as far as Velepromet was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you set off for Velepromet. At what time was that; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely. I do remember, though, that we walked on foot for quite a long time. And as I am -- usually say, that according to the regulations, military regulations, a soldier makes 66 steps a minute, we must have walked on foot for about an hour, definitely more than 40 minutes. I apologise, Mr. Vasic, but I was somewhat surprised by the fact that Major Sljivancanin said that a lance-corporal of the military police was to take us to the gate of Velepromet, where we were to be met by a superior officer, his subordinate, who was Captain First Class Srecko Borisavljevic, which means that he did not accompany us to hand the jurisdiction of the facility over to us, but, rather, he told us that we were to be made by Captain First Class Srecko Borisavljevic, who was informed of our imminent arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We seem to have trouble understanding each other, because you seem to be answering a question I did not put to you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you roughly when we arrived there, and then you can work out for yourself when it was that we set out. We arrived after 2200 hours. It must have been around 2230. Now, if we work back from there, we will arrive at the time of our departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you did not use the car that you had at your disposal. Why did you go on foot?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that we were to go on foot. We were told so by Major Sljivancanin. Why was that? Well, probably because this was a rather large group there. Major Muncan's group was also going with us, and that was a group of some four to five people. We could not fit into a car; we had to have at least a mini-bus or a regular bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The group that set out for Velepromet, how many people were there exactly?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that we were five of us in our group and there were about five of them in their group, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While you were on your way there, did you or the military police have any contact with the commander of the company?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Major Sljivancanin must have been in touch with them because he was their superior. He must have been in touch with them personally, and he must have had a radio communications or a telephone line with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, please answer my questions. We want to save time. I asked you about -- the question was about you, not about Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any radio equipment, any communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On your way from Negoslavci to Velepromet, did you come across any check-point manned by either the JNA, or did you come across a military police patrol?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were approaching the Velepromet gate, we came across buses holding women. There were several buses full of civilians, women, the elderly, and perhaps even children.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, you're deliberately answering in a way that does not answer my question.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answers are truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My question was whether you came across a JNA check-point or a military police patrol, and you're telling me about buses holding women and children.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by a JNA check-point? I don't understand that. Please clarify that and then I'll answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you stopped by a JNA check-point at some point or by a military police patrol?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were accompanied by a military police patrol. There was a lance-corporal who took us to the Velepromet gate together with his soldiers. The lance-corporal was assigned to that task by Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a curfew in Vukovar at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, in an area controlled by the military police, the military police are in charge of the curfew and we were being taken there by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that you arrived in Velepromet and you met Captain First Class Borisavljevic there; is that right? You also said that you held a meeting there with him and his officers, non-commissioned officers, forensic technicians, members of your own group, and was there perhaps a group of officers from the security administration of the 1st Military District there at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a whole lot of questions, isn't it? First of all, I reported. I then gained a quick insight into the situation that prevailed, and then I told Captain Borisavljevic to call all the officers to the meeting so that we could share their assignments with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Borisavljevic's officers, officers from Colonel Slavko Tomic's group, officers from Dragan Muncan's group, and it is now that we're getting to the bone of contention, which is probably what you're after, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were forensic technicians present at this meeting, too, those who were at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were these forensic people from the security administration?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. But there were those who were on duty from the security administration and the military court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that this meeting took place immediately after your arrival. Borisavljevic reported to you, and then you surveyed the situation. How much time elapsed between your arrival and the meeting, the time the meeting was called?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been about 15 minutes, 10 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did this meeting take place between 2300 hours and 2330 that evening, as you told the OTP investigator?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that sounds very likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you held this meeting, did you issue orders and instructions at the meeting on how the evacuation of the people from Velepromet should proceed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I relayed the order. The order comprised the following. First of all, we were to introduce ourselves, so we said: We are a group of senior officers from the security administration. Our assignment is to give you a hand with screening war criminals and separating them from blameless civilians. They immediately said: Colonel, this task has already been completed. The prisoners of war have already been separated from the civilians. My apologies. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: You say that at this point in time you were the leader of this group and you were in charge of carrying out this assignment, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That means you took over command, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I took over command from the moment that I told you about, the moment when I clearly stated: Listen, I now have command over this. Up to that point, I had been in control, but from this moment on I was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At this meeting, were you aware of how many people you had to help you carry out this assignment?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I realised how many people were available to me for this assignment, but what I didn't know was how many soldiers were available, with the exception of those specified by Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you not ask Captain Borisavljevic how many soldiers were available within the Velepromet compound?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not even my duty to ask him that. I heard this from Major Sljivancanin. He said -- do you want me to repeat what he said?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is this: When planning and carrying out an assignment, would not the first step be to establish how many men are available to you and then you decide on how you go about carrying out a certain assignment once you've established that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I do happen to know a thing or two about control and command. I didn't just happen to be there, and I wasn't there merely to check how things were going. I was there to give them a hand with carrying out this assignment. I was there to make sure that the assignment was carried out in keeping with the regulations and the plan, as set out to us by Major Sljivancanin. I was not aware of the plan's substance or objective, but I took Major Sljivancanin's word for it. I took his word for it that his military police unit would ensure that everything would be under control, as he said, and that everything would proceed according to regulations. He said we needn't worry, there wouldn't be any problems there, except ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except such problems as we had already experienced by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You testified about this before the war crimes district court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. First of all, I testified before the president of the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, I'm asking you a very specific question here. You're just wasting time, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Try to be more specific then, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I would like to show you a portion of the transcript from this trial. The page is 34 of the B/C/S. And for the benefit of my learned friends and the Chamber, the relevant pages in English are 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is it that you're not certain about, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please read out the passage that begins with your quote, "the person in control of that group."

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "The person in control of that group for the Velepromet assignment." If you read from there, it should be clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Vujic.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "For the Velepromet assignment," which means I agreed to this. I took over command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Did you testify to this effect at the Belgrade trial?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the Belgrade trial transcript, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need the transcript anymore now. If Mr. Usher could just take the transcript back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that you held a meeting. At this meeting, did you tell those present what their respective assignments were?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you give them individual assignments?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you tell them that once their assignments were completed, they should report back to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know how many people were involved in each of these assignments that you handed out to them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assignment was received by Colonel Tomic. The assignment was received was Colonel Kijanovic. The assignment was received by Captain First Class Borisavljevic. The assignment was received by two of his junior officers. The assignment was received by Branko Korica. The assignment was received by Slobodan Stosic to start boarding the POWs on the buses with the escort of the military police. I also told the commander when to begin boarding.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were assignments received by all the members of the 1st Military District group?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Muncan and Korica, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the rest of them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were involved. I even assigned two officers to some of the buses, simply because I didn't know the exact number of the POWs there as Major Sljivancanin had not told me. He was asked by Colonel Tomic at one point about the number of captured Ustashas, to quote him, and there was an additional question about the number of officers or leaders of these Ustashas, as he expressed himself at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Before you handed out these assignments and started implementing your assignment, did you check what sort of equipment was available to the units stationed at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a military police company, and they would have had sufficient automatic weapons to prevent them from being unpleasantly surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you check if there was any radio or telephone linked to the command post in Negoslavci or to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't part of my remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was it not within your remit before you actually got down to handing out assignments to -- and issuing an order for the prisoners to start boarding the buses to actually verify the situation in terms of the security aspect?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not within my remit. All of this was done by Major Sljivancanin, who was Colonel Mrksic's assistant for security. It was his duty to report to his superiors on the situation and any problems faced within the area of responsibility. I trusted the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you took responsibility for this assignment --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the area of responsibility of Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me finish, please. You took responsibility for this assignment. Did you not have to make sure first that there was sufficient forces available, that a security assessment was made, and wasn't it only then that you would be in a situation to order an evacuation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a position to consider threats to our mission, to our assignment, and potential sources for these threats. However, Major Sljivancanin clearly told me: You needn't worry. There are no special surprises in store for you. Everything is under control. There's a military police unit there under the command of Captain Borisavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you didn't speak to Captain Borisavljevic about Velepromet's security and how this was organised? I mean when he reported to you and later at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I inspected the compound together with Captain Borisavljevic. His officers were there and officers from both groups were there. The group under Captain Tomic and that under Major Muncan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, I'm asking you one thing; you're answering something altogether different. Did you look into the security of Captain Borisavljevic's unit? Did you look into the security situation throughout the Velepromet compound before you actually gave an order for the evacuation to commence?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, and there was no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know if there was a guards commander at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there was one. Do you know what the commander of a police company is, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I was asking you about the guards commander.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What guards commander are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So there was none, was there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. There was security at the highest possible level. This security was set up by Captain Borisavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you notice perhaps whether there were any TO staff members at Velepromet or any police members, police officers, belonging to the government of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Major Sljivancanin replied to Colonel Tomic about the number of Ustashas and their whereabouts, he stated that the exact number was not known. He said that they had been gradually surrendering in various places, in various buildings, that they were mingling with the civilians and that this was how they had reached Velepromet. He said there were about 2.000 people there, civilians for the most part, women, children.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Vujic. I asked you about any TO staff members, Vukovar TO staff members. I asked you about Vukovar's police members, not about the Croatian forces or about the women or about the children.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm answering your question, Mr. Vasic. He said: Everybody's mingling in Velepromet. It's all mixed up. You have civilians there, prisoners of war, as well as TO members. He didn't distinguish between those. He just said "TO members." He had it all mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But did you see for yourself, perhaps later on, that there were people from the TO staff and from the TO there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I was not aware of the existence of the TO staff to begin with until I actually saw the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You also realised while there that the chief of police, Crevar, was holding people there, people he had captured and people he was now screening for war crimes or investigating?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please hear me out. I'll try to repeat exactly what I said in my statement; I'll try to repeat exactly what I said before this Chamber. When I held a meeting, heads were popping in and out through the door, bearded faces, wearing the kind of uniform that you have described. I asked: Who are these people? Who are these people? Borisavljevic and his junior officers, his subordinates said: These people are here with us. These people are from the TO staff. I was appalled by their behaviour, and naturally I asked: What are these people doing here? If they're chiefs from the TO staff, they should have attended the meeting in the first place, but they were not attending the meeting. I only realised they were there when they started muttering, as we say in the army, about what prisoners of war are these people talking about? What buses? These people are not leaving. They were mumbling on and on about this out in the corridor. And then when I started inspecting the compound, the first room I came across had twice as many guards outside as usual, the one I told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let's leave these rooms alone for the time being. When you found out that these people were not part of the meeting, the meeting that was in progress, when you realised they were mumbling and complaining about your decisions, why did you not have them removed from the room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I possibly have wanted to have them removed if Borisavljevic was assuring me that these people were there with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat exactly what these people were saying.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said our task was to separate the prisoners of war from the civilians, to get them onto the buses once the buses were there, to do this immediately, to do this as soon as possible, they said: All of this has already been done. The POWs were separated from the civilians. Only some women were left within the compound. I can describe it for you if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the triage. I didn't ask you about the women. I asked you what the TO staff members were grumbling about as you were when the meeting was in progress?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you already. You're not taking these people away. What buses are you talking about, what prisoner of wars? Those were the words they were using as they were grumbling out in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you heard them grumbling about this, why did you not take steps to have these people removed from the Velepromet compound?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I have if this had never been ordered by Colonel Mrksic or Major Sljivancanin? Was I there to arrest the Vukovar chief of police? Wouldn't that strike you as slightly strange in the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you took over command, you took over responsibility for the assignment, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I completed my assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It was your duty to implement the assignment and to create conditions that would not jeopardise your assignment?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not my duty. It was Colonel Mrksic's duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Colonel Mrksic didn't hear any grumbling, you did.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he did, too. All of these people were within --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me please conclude my question, and after that would you please make a break so that the interpreters can catch up. In addition, I would also ask you to answer my questions directly. From whom could Mr. Mrksic at that time, at 11.00 p.m., hear that members of the TO staff were grumbling in front of the meeting where you were -- in front of the room where you were holding a meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How come these people ended up in the area of responsibility of Colonel Mrksic and Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you're claiming that you had no duty whatsoever to take preventive action in view of the threats issued by the TO staff members. Didn't you have to remove them from Velepromet? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Clarify, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they specifically endangered the implementation of the combat assignment, then yes, it would have been my duty to take the responsibilities, as regulated by law and apply force. I will describe to you how I applied force.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This will do for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect to my learned friend. He asked the question. He may not wish to have the second part. But the question was asked and half the answer is given. Surely the witness should be entitled to give the reason why either yes or no applied. My learned friend says: "Clarify, please." And if they specifically endangered, then he said he would apply force. So I would submit that, in actual fact, the reply: "This will do for the time being" is trying to cut off the witness in giving a full explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness was going on to say: How I applied force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which is a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At the meeting which you held at Velepromet, did you say that the implementation of the task is something that you were taking over on behalf of the security administration and the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Given this fact, did you hear from Captain Borisavljevic what forces -- what resources were available to you to conduct the evacuation, how many people there were at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear how many prisoners of war there were, nor did I hear how many buses would arrive or how many people he had under him. I knew how many people there generally were in a military police company, and I also knew what firing capabilities they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that at the meeting you assigned tasks on behalf of the security administration and the Supreme Command. Did you create a plan as to where the buses would line up once they arrived?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The plan was already in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of this plan?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who decided how the buses would be boarded, in which order, in which way, and where the buses would be lined up once they arrived?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ordered the buses to enter the Velepromet compound. I ordered when the buses should leave the compound. I said that the facilities with prisoners of war ought to be emptied gradually in accordance with the regulation that the subordinate officers that I described who had taken over the assignment were in charge of that, and that they were supposed to write down, if possible, how many prisoners of war they boarded on to which bus, to write down the name of the driver and the licence plate of the bus and to report to me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, you created the specific plan for this evacuation.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I simply assigned specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you saw these people from the TO staff popping up and making comments, were you able to see how many there were and where they were?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Later on I met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you started implementing the assignment of evacuation, when you had toured the facilities at Velepromet, what was your security assessment? Did you conclude that you had sufficient manpower to conduct the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I concluded that the situation was under control, that there would be obstruction from the members of the TO staff and the Chetnik unit when in front of the room where I found what they described as 45 Ustashas and criminals of war, I found a double set of guards in front of that room comprising three members of the Chetnik unit with sub-machine-guns and two members of military police with sub-machine-guns who were shoving each other in front of that room. The Chetniks did not allow me to look into the room. This room had a tin door with -- with blinds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Chetniks and police members were shoving each other. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were pushing each other with their shoulders. All of them were quite tall, about 190, and they had their backs turned to me. They were facing the room, so they were pushing each other to place themselves closer to the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could it be said that the JNA soldiers were actually trying to take up the positions occupied by the Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be described that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you saw that, did you order the Chetniks to step aside, to move away from that area?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I asked, prior to that, Captain Borisavljevic who these people were. He said that they were there as well, that is to say, that they had placed their security people there and that they had already started some kind of proceedings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you disregarded this fact that the JNA members and the Chetniks were shoving each other and that the Chetniks were not allowing you to -- allowing you to look into the room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did look into the room, and I did so by telling Zvonko Cekic, the second lieutenant, that he should enable me to look into the room. I told him that in front of Borisavljevic, and he did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And so what did you see once you looked into the room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were heads popping up, the heads of prisoners of war, that they described as Ustashas and war criminals. They needed air. These people had injured faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Once you saw that they had facial injuries, why didn't you remove the Chetnik security officers there and take these people out in order to assist them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked the doctor who reported to me at the infirmary -- I don't know who set it up, whether it was the TO staff or the units of Colonel Mrksic. So I asked this doctor whether he provided any first aid. He said: Yes, I -- and he also said that he had helped some people more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, you looked inside, took stock of what was going on in the room and then you moved elsewhere, leaving the Chetniks there in front of the room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just the Chetniks. Also the JNA military police unit, the unit under command of Captain Borisavljevic who was in charge of the security at this facility. Captain Borisavljevic was constantly accompanying me while I toured the rooms where the POWs were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this way: Who stayed there to provide security, to guard this room after you left?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police and the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Didn't you suppose that the Chetniks would create additional problems once you came again to inspect the room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I can describe exactly what problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you think that they would create further problems?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need for me to expect. I can describe to you, and let me just describe to you what I experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the measures you took prior to the incident occurring. I'm asking you about your security assessment, and then I'm asking you whether you should have supposed that these same Chetniks would create new problems once you came once again to take the people out of this room with tin door.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could have supposed that there would be further problems, but I also could have supposed that I wasn't going to come here and testify, but that, rather, that I would be five feet under ground, just like other people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you said that you could have supposed that something like this could happen, did you, in your view, have sufficient manpower to thwart their obstruction?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had sufficient manpower. I had full trust in them, and I accomplished my assignment with these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you say that you accomplished your task, does this mean that all prisoners of war who were at Velepromet were evacuated pursuant to your orders and left these facilities?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense that I took stock of the situation and boarded people on the buses, in that sense, yes, I did accomplish my task. As for those people who were abducted and who died behind the compound of Velepromet, then yes, I didn't manage to save these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Given that fact, wouldn't you say that you didn't accomplish your?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did accomplish the task. I could have ended my life there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If there were persons who were imprisoned there and if these persons were taken out by somebody and killed, wasn't it because you did not take control of the situation and create conditions necessary for evacuation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept your thesis, and I find it quite offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in which order did you tour the facilities where prisoners of war were held?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first place to which Borisavljevic and Sekic took me was the room where, according to Marko Crevar and Vojvoda Topola, people they described as Ustashas and criminals, slaughtering Serbs were held. They also said that they had already taken steps against these people and that these people had to be held accountable for what they had done.
